title: The Microscope Lab
summary: Snap a sharp, enlarged photo of a bug with a magnifier, then crack the two dials of a compound microscope.
subject: physics
concepts: The near point of the eye
learningOutcome: The student can place an object for a magnifier so the image is at the near point, find m = 1 + D/f, and set a compound microscope’s object distance and tube length for a wanted magnification.

levels.title: Bug safari
levels.adds: Baseline: put the object inside f so the image sits at the near point: u = fD/(f + D) and m = 1 + D/f (Ex 9.22 to 9.24).
hints: The most magnified sharp picture has its virtual image exactly at the near point, 25 cm from the lens.
With v = −25 cm use 1/u = 1/v − 1/f, or u = fD/(f + D).
The magnification there is m = 1 + D/f, which is also the magnifying power.

levels.title: Cracking the microscope
levels.adds: New idea: total magnification is m_o × (1 + D/f_e) at the near point; two dials set u_o and the tube length (Ex 9.11, 9.12, 9.26).
hints: The eyepiece alone gives 1 + D/f_e, so the objective must give m_o = M ÷ (1 + D/f_e).
For the objective, u_o = f_o(1 + 1/m_o) and v_o = m_o u_o.
The eyepiece’s object is at u_e = f_e D/(f_e + D) from it, so the tube length is L = v_o + u_e.

misconceptions: The magnifying power of a magnifier is the same thing as its linear magnification in every position
A magnifying glass of very short focal length can magnify without limit
The eyepiece of a microscope makes a real image on the retina side of the lens
